Feature Description: A free-text note box on the prescription, printed in its own section separate from the patient advice, so the doctor can record an instruction to the pharmacy or a reminder for the next visit. The note forms part of the signed record: once the consultation is signed it is corrected by adding a dated amendment rather than by overwriting what was originally written.

X-ray and pathology set up as departments with their own staff, who receive test requests raised by doctors during a consultation rather than taking appointments. Department staff attach the X-ray image or the report against the patient's request, and it becomes available to the ordering doctor at once - during the current visit and afterwards in the patient's history - so nobody carries a film or a printout between rooms. This depends on secure document storage: every file encrypted, reachable only by the clinic that owns it, and every view recorded.

Staff can correct a patient's details - name, age, gender, mobile number, address - after registration. At present these are locked once the patient is created, so a mistyped mobile number cannot be fixed and the clinic loses the ability to contact that patient. Every correction records who made it, when, and what the value was before. Records are never deleted; a patient registered twice is merged into a single file so the full treatment history stays together.

Financial records cannot be edited or deleted. A mistake is corrected by posting a reversing entry that refers to the original, so nothing in the clinic's books can be changed silently. Only an administrator can post a correction, and must record a reason for it - front desk staff can collect payments but cannot reverse, waive or refund them. The invoice itself shows what was corrected, by whom, when and why.

While seeing a patient, the doctor can view the previous visit - date, diagnosis, medicines with dosage, and vitals - without leaving the consultation screen. Today the doctor has to navigate away to check what was prescribed last time, which interrupts the consultation and risks losing unsaved notes. The doctor can also carry the previous visit's medicines into today's prescription in one click and edit them before signing, which is how most follow-up visits are handled.
